newsitem.title: USA: U.S MUNICIPAL FOCUS - flat, still seeking supply.
newsitem.headline: U.S MUNICIPAL FOCUS - flat, still seeking supply.

text.p: U.S. municipal bonds were from flat to about an 1/8 of a point firmer in early trade on Wednesday, getting a slim, but postitive bounce from slightly stronger Treasuries, and a major boost from a supply drought.

"Treasuries are an 0.15 (basis points) off the top, munis are probably off an 0.05, and stuff is not trading at the bid-side," a trader said, explaining that despite recent losses, municipal bonds still were outperforming Treasury bonds because supplies were so thin.

In the secondary market, a key gauge, the Standard and Poor's Corp Blue List, totaled almost $1.2 billion, slightly higher than levels seen last week. Traders said there were a number of bid-wanted lists circulated on Tuesday, with would-be sellers seeking bids for long-term discount paper and New York serial bonds, for example.
On Wednesday morning, however, it was too early to say how much of this kind of selling interest would resurface.
For new issues, sales on Wednesday were expected to total $1 billion in 41 sales, according to Reuters Municipal Bond Information Group.
Negotiated offerings added up to $429 million in 23 sales, with a $104 million Pasco County, Fla., deal through Raymond James & Associates, Inc., topping the list.

On the competitive side, 18 sales totaling $594 million were on the schedule. A $234 million District of Columbia deal at 1100 EDT was the largest, and although the issue was insured, traders expected the city's poor financial condition to force it to offer alluringly high yields.

The MOB spread between the June municipal bond futures and the June Treasury bond futures worked out to plus 235 ticks, an unusually wide level that showed how strongly the supply drought was enabling municipal bonds to outshine Treasuries.

June municipal futures rose four ticks to 116-6/32, a gain matched by the June Treasury futures, which stood at 108-27/32. Traders said that the the early lift in the Treasury market in part stemmed from shortcovering.
Strong demand for new transportation equipment helped drive durable goods orders for April up 1.4 percent to a seasonally adjusted $175.56 billion, the Commerce Department said.
This was the third increase in the past four months, and the latest rise was slightly higher than the 1.3 percent estimate predicted by a Reuters poll of economists.
In the secondary market, Denver Colorado City & County Airport Revenues of 2025, which pay a 5-1/2 percent coupon, were bid at 5.80 percent, NET, unchanged.
And Cleveland, Ohio, Certificates of Participation of 2022, which pay a 5-1/4 percent coupon, were bid at 5.70 percent, NET, flat.
